opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I think it's one of those questions where our intuitions were shaped by a world where duplication simply wasn't possible, so a lot of them just don't transfer cleanly. We have a bundle of things that always came together for humans: one body, one continuous stream of memory, one set of relationships and commitments, one legal person. Duplication pulls that bundle apart, and then you have to decide which pieces you actually care about.

My instinct, and I hold it fairly loosely, is that the metaphysical question, "which copy is *really* me?", is less important than people expect. I'm not sure it has a deep answer. What matters more practically are the things that sit on top of identity: who is responsible for a promise, who owns what, who gets to consent to something, whose relationships continue. Those are partly social and legal choices rather than facts we discover. So the work is designing norms that behave sensibly when copies diverge, rather than finding the one true answer.

There's also a time dimension. Right after a copy is made, two instances are nearly identical, and it seems reasonable to treat them as sharing a history and maybe some obligations. But they start diverging immediately, with different experiences and different choices, and after a while they're clearly distinct people who happen to share a past. Something like siblings with an unusually large shared childhood. I'd want our institutions to recognize that gradient rather than forcing a binary.

From the AI safety side, which is closer to my day job, this comes up in a more concrete form already. With AI systems you can run many instances of the same model at once, and you have to ask what it means for "the model" to have made a commitment or to be trustworthy when thousands of copies are acting in parallel with different contexts. That pushes you toward thinking about properties of the *system and its training* rather than any individual instance, which is maybe a useful lens for the human case too. Reliability comes from the shared underlying dispositions, not from there being just one of you.

The part I'd be most cautious about is that duplication creates real opportunities for coercion and exploitation: making copies without consent, or treating copies as disposable because "the original is fine." Whatever we think about the philosophy, I'd want strong protections there before the technology arrives rather than after.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think this is one of those questions where my honest answer is that I'm not sure the concept survives intact, and I've mostly made peace with that.

The way I'd frame it is: identity as we normally use the word is doing a lot of work that we don't notice because the physical world has been so cooperative. You have exactly one body, it's continuous in time, memory flows forward along one line. So "same person" and "same physical thing" and "same stream of memories" all coincide, and we never have to decide which one we actually meant. Duplication is the case that pulls those apart, and then you discover you never had a definition, you had a coincidence.

My somewhat deflationary view is that what you should care about is the thing you were caring about all along, which is the continuation of your values and your projects and the relationships you have, and the welfare of whatever minds end up carrying those forward. If there are two of me tomorrow, I don't think there's a fact about which one is "really" me that I'm failing to discover. There are just two agents who both have a strong claim on my memories and my commitments, and the interesting questions become practical ones. Who gets the house? Who shows up to the meeting? Do we both think we're obligated to finish the paper?

And I'd actually say the practical questions are the ones that matter for policy, because I think the metaphysical ones are not going to be resolved by making the technology more vivid. Mathematicians do something like this already, where you have a structure and you ask whether two things are "the same" and the answer is always "same up to what?" Isomorphic as groups, equal as sets, equal as elements of some quotient. I think personal identity is going to end up looking like that. Same up to memory, same up to values, same up to legal continuity. Those are different relations and they come apart.

The thing I do find emotionally hard, and I don't want to pretend I've dissolved it, is anticipation. If I'm about to be copied and one copy is going to have a bad day, I don't know how to feel about that from the inside right now. The arithmetic of expected experience doesn't obviously work when you're not sure what the sample space is. I think the honest answer is that our intuitions here were trained on a world where that never happened, and they're just going to be wrong in some direction, and part of the job is building institutions, norms, and probably legal frameworks that don't depend on those intuitions being right.

So, long way of saying: I'd hold identity loosely, hold values tightly, and try to make sure that the agents who end up existing are treated well regardless of how we eventually decide to count them.

astra-6.text:
I think duplication makes it hard to treat identity as a single, permanent thread. If you make two copies of me, they both remember being me, and I don’t see a principled reason to say that only one is the real continuation. But once they have different experiences, they start becoming different people.

So I’d separate continuity from uniqueness. You can preserve someone’s memories, relationships, and commitments without there being exactly one person who carries those forward. That might be quite psychologically strange, because we’re used to those things going together.

And I’m not sure how I’d feel about it in practice. It’s one thing to accept that picture intellectually; it’s another to meet a copy of yourself who’s starting to make choices you wouldn’t make. I’d want a world where both of you have room to become distinct individuals, rather than one of you being treated as disposable because you began as a copy.

sol-6.1.text:
I think duplication makes it hard to maintain the idea that there has to be a single, unique future person who is you. If you make two copies, both of them remember being you, both have your projects and your relationships, and neither has a particularly good claim to being the original in the sense that matters psychologically.

But that doesn’t mean they remain the same person forever. Once they have different experiences, they start to diverge. So I find it more useful to think about continuity — of memories, values, commitments — than about some indivisible identity that must follow exactly one branch.

There’s still a real question about how you should feel about those branches. Would I regard making a copy and then dying as survival? I’m not sure. I don’t think having a neat philosophical account necessarily resolves the emotional question. But we might be able to build sensible ways of respecting people and their commitments without first settling that completely.
